question: In 2019, Veolia purchased a landfill site in Barrancabermeja, Colombia. Since then, work done by NGOs has revealed that Veolia has committed serious violations of human and environmental rights. Untreated pollutants are being discharged into a protected wetland that feeds several rivers and provides drinking water to 300 000 people.

The end result: heavy metals are seeping into the environment, with mercury levels 25 times higher than the maximum permissible limit, and this in a corridor designated as a feline protection area. This poisoning of the ecosystem is causing cancer, kidney and brain damage, and congenital malformations in infants. There has been wholesale disappearance of wildlife and it is now impossible to fish.
Several whistleblowers have had to flee the region after being threatened by paramilitary groups allegedly in cahoots with the multinational. Will the Commission therefore: 1.
Take cognisance of its moral failure, given its desire to totally dismantle the directive on corporate sustainability due diligence for big companies?
Monitor and sanction violations of environmental and fundamental rights, along with Veolia’s corporate accountability obligations?
Ensure the necessary protection is provided for the activists and whistle-blowers involved?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.2.2026) In its proposal COM(2025) 81 final1, which also amended Directive (EU) 2024/1760 (Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive – CSDDD)2, the Commission aimed at retaining the Directive’s core elements and upholding its objectives, and defended its proposal during the interinstitutional negotiations of the Omnibus I.

The final text of the CSDDD reflects the agreement reached by the co-legislators. It preserves the due diligence obligation for large companies to address adverse human rights and environmental impacts globally – within their operations, those of their subsidiaries, and across their chains of activities.

Compliance with the CSDDD will be subject to public enforcement by Member States, which shall designate independent supervisory authorities with adequate investigatory and enforcement powers. The Commission will set up a European Network of Supervisory Authorities to ensure coordination and cooperation at EU level.

The Directive provides for victims’ right to full compensation, as well as measures to facilitate access to justice. The CSDDD stresses the importance of safeguarding activists and whistle-blowers. This includes ensuring that engagement processes are free from retaliation and retribution, with an emphasis on maintaining confidentiality and anonymity.

Safeguards are also provided where these persons submit substantiated concerns to supervisory authorities or file complaints (or notifications) directly with companies. Further protection is granted under Directive (EU) 2019/19373, which also covers the reporting of breaches of national laws transposing the CSDDD.
While the CSDDD – following its amendment – will start to apply in July 2029, some Member States, such as France, already have national laws on sustainability due diligence in place.
